No, that's not right, and it matters for your design. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own.

It's a tempting idea because chatbots seem to remember. Within one chat, the app resends the whole conversation to the model on every turn. The model isn't remembering anything. It re-reads the transcript each time. This follows from what you already showed in your notes: the model only knows its training plus the text it is given right now.

You can see the same thing in code:

- Student A chats on Monday. The program sends the model the manuals and Monday's messages.
- The conversation ends, and the model keeps nothing.
- Student A returns the next week. The program starts a new call with only the new message. The model has no idea who they are or what they said.

The memory has to live in your program, not in the model. For example:

- At the end of a session, your code saves the useful facts to a file or database. One example is "Sam finished laser cutter training on Oct 12."
- When Sam comes back, your code loads that record and puts it into the text it sends to the model.
- Then the model can use it, because it is now in its input.

In computer science terms, the model is like a stateless function: the same input gives the same kind of output, and nothing persists between calls. Your saved records are the database. The analogy breaks down in one way: the model's input has a size limit, so you can't paste in everything a student ever said.

That limit is the next topic. It also matters for your budget, since longer input costs more.

Quick check: for the makerspace assistant, what would you save about each student, and where in the flow would your code put it back in front of the model?
